n: Just days after the wall is finished, the people gather “as one man” and ask Ezra to bring out the law of Moses. The request comes from the people themselves — they are hungry for God’s word.

f.w: the book of the law of Moses
f.g: Probably the five books of Moses (Genesis–Deuteronomy) or a large part of them.

n: Ezra brings the law before men, women, and children old enough to understand. It is the first day of the seventh month, the Feast of Trumpets.

f.w: the first day of the seventh month
all that could hear with understanding
f.g: Including older children who could follow along.

n: Ezra reads aloud from dawn until noon — about six hours — and everyone listens closely. Few people had copies of scripture, so hearing it read was precious.

f.w: the ears of all the people were attentive

n: Ezra stands on a wooden platform built for the occasion, with thirteen leaders beside him, showing unity and support for the reading.

f.g: A raised wooden platform so all could see and hear.

n: When Ezra unrolls the scroll, the whole crowd stands up out of reverence for God’s word.

f.g: Standing for the reading of scripture became a lasting custom in synagogues.

n: Ezra praises God, and the people answer “Amen, Amen,” raising their hands, then bowing low in worship. The reading of scripture becomes an act of worship.

f.g: “So be it, truly” — a doubled, wholehearted agreement.

n: Levites move among the people to help them understand, while the crowd stays in place. Hearing God’s word is not enough; it must be understood.

f.w: caused the people to understand the law

n: They read clearly and explained the meaning. Many scholars think this included translating the Hebrew into Aramaic, the everyday language most exiles now spoke.

f.g: Clearly, or possibly “with interpretation” — translating into Aramaic.

n: As they understand the law, the people weep — realizing how far they had fallen short. But their leaders tell them not to mourn, because this is a holy feast day.

Nehemiah tells them to celebrate with rich food and sweet drinks and to share with those who have nothing. “The joy of the LORD is your strength” — godly joy, not only sorrow, gives power to keep going.

f.w: eat the fat, and drink the sweet
f.g: Enjoy the best foods and sweet drinks.

f.w: send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared
the joy of the LORD is your strength

n: The Levites calm the crowd: be quiet and don’t grieve, for the day is holy.
The people go home to feast, share, and rejoice. Their joy came from understanding — the word of God, once understood, brought happiness.

f.w: because they had understood the words

n: The next day, the family heads, priests, and Levites return to study further with Ezra. Leaders went deeper in study so they could lead their families well.

f.w: even to understand the words of the law

n: In their study they discover the commandment to live in temporary shelters during the Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh month.

f.g: Temporary shelters made of branches; the Hebrew word is sukkot.

f.w: the feast of the seventh month

n: So they announce it everywhere: go to the hills and gather branches to make booths. The feast reminded Israel that they had lived in shelters in the wilderness under God’s care.

f.g: The hill country, likely including the Mount of Olives.

n: The people build booths everywhere — on flat rooftops, in courtyards, at the temple, and in public squares. The whole city becomes a festival campground.

f.w: upon the roof of his house
f.g: Houses had flat roofs used as living space.
A gate on the north side of the city, facing toward the land of Ephraim.

n: Not since Joshua’s day had Israel kept the feast in quite this way, with everyone joining in such joy. The phrase stresses the uniqueness of this renewal more than total neglect before.

f.g: Joshua, Moses’ successor; “Jeshua” is another spelling of his name.

n: Ezra reads the law every day of the seven-day feast, ending with a solemn assembly on the eighth day, as Moses commanded. The law also required a reading of the law at this feast every seventh year.
